open_obligations: Note that the judges are LLMs, and check whether the errors here are the kind of misleading errors Wen et al. call for evaluating.
Check whether consultant training here is analogous to RLHF in Wen et al.
Check whether debate actually reduced false positives on incorrect answers.
in.other_title: Debate training adds quoted evidence and transfers to GPT-4o; consultancy does not
in.rationale: Wen et al. ask whether scalable oversight methods such as debate work against misleading errors. Arnesen et al. report trained debaters add 96% more quoted words and their win rates transfer between judges (correlation 0.98), while trained consultants' transfer only at 0.51, which the authors read as consultants learning features idiosyncratically convincing to their judge; the judges are LLMs (a trained GPT-4-Turbo judge and an untrained GPT-4o judge).
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate resists the judge-specific persuasion that one-sided optimisation learns, for trained Llama3-8B debaters and consultants

text: The authors note that scalable oversight work has explored model assistance for human evaluators via task decomposition, test case generation, critique and debate, but that apart from Saunders et al. (2022) most such work lacks evaluation on subtle, misleading errors. They call for future work to evaluate the real-world effectiveness of these techniques, particularly on misleading errors, and to deploy them at scale.
title: Do scalable oversight methods (critique, debate, decomposition) work on misleading errors?
